messages.subject: Input to rmr2 - Questions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to ask a few questions that are related on the input of rmr2. My questions are:

1. in the tutorial ( https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/rmr2/blob/master/docs/tutorial.md ) it is mentioned that "It is not possible to write out big data with to.dfs, not in a scalable way.". What does this mean ? If I want to write for example 4 TB of data then it is not efficient?
2. The default input when to.dfs is used is with null key and the value contains the data. This way only one map function is called. If I have large amount of data (e.g. 4TB) then what will happen ? Only one map function will be called ?
3. If I want to change the default key,value pair and define my own key but the value is the same, how can I do this efficiently ? For example, if I have a dataset and the key defines different columns of the dataset and the value is the whole dataset, how can I do it efficiently ?
4. If I want to change the input format to the mapreduce then the whole dataset would be processed ? E.g. if I use make.input.format.

These are some questions that bothering me for some time now.
If someone knows please answer me.

Thank you in advanced

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Mar 1, 2014 at 10:29 PM, Panagiotis Tzirakis <tzir...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I would like to ask a few questions that are related on the input of rmr2. My questions are:
>
> 1. in the tutorial ( https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/rmr2/blob/master/docs/tutorial.md ) it is mentioned that "It is not possible to write out big data with to.dfs, not in a scalable way.". What does this mean ? If I want to write for example 4 TB of data then it is not efficient?

It's not even a matter of efficient. The data would need to be in memory first. At current cost for RAM, that would set you back some $65K, assuming that you could mount all those modules into one system. If you have 4 TB of data, your only option is mapreduce (the call).

> 2. The default input when to.dfs is used is with null key and the value contains the data. This way only one map function is called.

I don't believe there is a relation, but then change the key, be my guest. It's only a default.

> If I have large amount of data (e.g. 4TB) then what will happen ? Only one map function will be called ?

No, the machine would have crashed long before you can even type to.dfs. You will never be in a position to test this.

> 3. If I want to change the default key,value pair and define my own key but the value is the same, how can I do this efficiently ?

You can't change the default key, but you can provide the first argument, indeed the key, as in

to.dfs(keyval(key, value))

> For example, if I have a dataset and the key defines different columns of the dataset and the value is the whole dataset, how can I do it efficiently ?

You can't because you don't have enough RAM. You are completely misunderstanding the role of to.dfs. It ships data from memory to the distributed file system. Memory is limited to 10s of GBs in most systems. 10GB is not big data unless you are asking some marketer with a fervent imagination.

> 4. If I want to change the input format to the mapreduce then the whole dataset would be processed ?

Depending on the input format.  The input format function could stop reading before the first record. But most reasonable input formats will try and read all the way to the end, unless there is an error of course.

> E.g. if I use make.input.format.

> If someone knows please answer me.

I hope this helps.

Antonio

Hi all,

map <- function(k,v) {
    fields <- unlist(strsplit(v, ","))
    kv_map = keyval(fields[1],fields[3])

    return(kv_map)
}

  input = "test_stock.txt",
  input.format = "text",

fields <- unlist(strsplit(v, ","))
    kv_map = keyval(fields[1],fields[3])

These two lines parse only the first line and discard the rest. Why not use

input.format = make.input.format("csv", sep = ",")

Then v is a data frame and you just return

keyval(v[,1], v[,3])

Plus you are not using any of the debugging possibilities. Absolutely run this on the local backend with a local file. Enter debug(map). Run. There's a whole debugging guide on the wiki. Don't make your life more difficult than it has to be.

Antonio

Hi Antonio,

Thanks for your kindly reply.
I tried the code you suggested, and it works fine now.
Sorry about my unclear concepts of Data Frame, list, and vector.

And right now going further, say I want the mean of v[3] and v[6] on each raw to be the value.(v[1] as key)
Intuitively I tried keyval(v[,1], mean(v[,3],v[,6])) in the map function, and unsurprisingly it failed...

However when I tried keyval(v[,1], (v[,3]+v[,6])/2), it worked.
Is there any way that I can use the mean() function?

And there's another question, I found that the final result showed in console is not sorted.
Is that because rmr2 cannot control the way Hadoop doing a map/reduce job?
(Though as long as the key/value correspond correctly, it's not a big issue...)

Here's my code & result using the same data set:

map <- function(k,v) {
  keyval(v[,1], (v[,3]+v[,6])/2)
}
from.dfs(
  mapreduce( input = "test_stock.txt",   input.format = make.input.format("csv", sep = ","),   map = map, )
)

messages.subject: Runtine issues after combining several MR jobs
messages.subject_clean: Runtine issues after combining several MR jobs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

after a major refactoring in my project I'm facing massive runtime changes and I'm a little clueless what causes them.

For development I divided my project into two MR-jobs:

1.
The first just did some calculations in the map phase an stored the result into the HDFS, no reduce phase.

2.
The second job read the data of the first job, and joined them with some additional information for subsequent comparison calculations and passed the results to the reducers where the comparisons were calculated and saved to the HDFS.

After making sure all the results and intermediate results are correct, I refactored my project. The map phases of both MR-jobs were joined, such that the calculations of the first mapper were joined with the data of the second mapper in one run an directly passed to the reducer. I expected this to be faster than the first set up since it saves the reading and writing to HDFS between the two MR-jobs. But unfortunately the opposite happened. A job lasting 29min in the old set up now takes now takes 66min. The extract of the log below shows mapping and reducing is done quite fast, progress is reported every few seconds. But finally the after  map 100%  reduce 100% it takes 52min to finish the job and I have no clue why.

Is it the cleaning that takes so much longer because of the intermediate results that have to be cleared now and may not reside in the HDFS between the MR-jobs?

I'm using rmr2-2.2.0, are there any known issues which could cause that behavior and an upgrade will promise some improvement?

Hopefully the information I gave is enough to understand and determine the cause of the slowdown.

Best,
Claudio

messages.body_plain:
I share your expectation that the combined job should be in general faster, all else being equal, than two separate jobs. Unfortunately I do not understand your attempted explanation. Not writing intermediate results is faster than writing them, it's a pretty general result in computing and life that not doing something takes shorter than doing it. The general principle in this group is that if you post a reproducible example you get help, if you don't you get sympathy and wild guesses at best. Your post is in the second category.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
I think rmr should clean up the tmp files it creates in the local file system.

If I understand correctly, there are global, local, map, combine and reduce environments created, saved and disseminated across the cluster for each mapreduce call.
As far as I could see, they are not reused after the initial call. So it would make sense (and would be considered good practice) for rmr to clean up after itself when the run is complete.

Am I missing anything?

Thanks!
-Saar

P.S. great job on the new release!

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1327] Temp file cleanup
messages.body_plain:
Hi Saar,
rmr uses exclusively temporary files as returned by tempfile(). Since those are cleared at the end of the session, it was never considered paramount to add additional logic to have them deleted earlier, but since some environment files can be big, maybe it wouldn't be such a bad idea to look into it. I notice nonetheless copy of those files accumulating when I am using standalone mode in Hadoop. My guess is that it is a Hadoop bug, but I never bothered reporting it so I am  not sure. In theory a running job is assigned a working directory that starts clean and is removed at the end (it's a feature called distributed cache). All the files rmr distributed to HDFS should be in that directory. This clearly is not happening at least in some instances. Therefore I would suggest that you open an issue on the rmr issue tracker, provide some example names for those files and their complete path and also I would like to know in which mode you are running hadoop. This is harder to fix than it seems since tasks may share some of those files, so I am not sure I can just delete them after reading them. The master R instance doesn't know where they are, the location being under Hadoop controls, and I am not sure I have API access to that piece of information. Anyway thanks for the report and we'll try to get to the bottom of it.

Antonio

I'm not sure we're talking about the same files, so I'll make sure before I go ahead and create an issue in the tracker: I was referring to the files created locally (map.file, reduce.file, combine.file, rmr.local.env, and rmr.global.env). When I run a long sequences of iterative mapreduce jobs (k-means iterations, for example) with different parameter values (number of clusters, starting values, dataset generating parameters) I get an accumulation of files in the local file system, under the current sessions' temporary directory. True, it should be cleaned up when the session ends, but It's been more than once that I've run out of space during long sessions...

I know I can address it by assigning ample space for these temp files and directing there using TMPDIR, TEMP or TMP, but I think (and I've been told by my cluster admin) that it would be good form for my own application to clean up after itself. These file names are available inside rmr.stream(), but are not accessible from outside that function (I think). It would be nice to have them deleted after the try.catch(system(...)) call.

(I'm using a 12 node Hortonworks hadoop cluster, not a standalone setup, but I think this is not what we're talking about. If the cluster configuration actually matters, I'd gladly post the relevant settings)

-Saar

messages.subject: Questions about equijoin
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to run a task in rmr that is element-wise multiplication of two big matrices. Suppose I have two big data matrices A and B and i have sent them to hdfs by to.dfs(). To make it simple, I use some small sample data here to illustrate.

Matrix A on hdfs
$key
[1] 118476480_1    118476480_7721 187108862_1    187108862_7721
Levels: 118476480_1 118476480_7721 187108862_1 187108862_7721

$val
          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] 15.721373 15.721373
[2,]  1.934481  1.934481
[3,] 27.301883 27.301883
[4,]  1.047634  1.047634

Matrix B on hdfs
$key
[1] 118476480_1    118476480_7721 187108862_1    187108862_7721
Levels: 118476480_1 118476480_7721 187108862_1 187108862_7721

$val
       [,1]   [,2]
[1,] 0.8911 0.9414
[2,] 0.8913 0.9413
[3,] 0.8911 0.9414
[4,] 0.8913 0.9413

Then i use equijoin to read and join them into one (key,val). the code is as follows.

A.B <- equijoin(
 left.input = A,
 right.input = B,
 map.left = function(k,v){
  keyval(k,v)
 },
 map.right = function(k,v){
  keyval(k,v)
 },
 outer = c("left")
)

from.dfs(A.B)

$key
NULL

$val
         V1.l      V2.l   V1.r   V2.r
1    1.934481  1.934481 0.8913 0.9413
1.1 27.301883 27.301883 0.8911 0.9414
1.2 15.721373 15.721373 0.8911 0.9414
1.3  1.047634  1.047634 0.8913 0.9413

At last, I used a mapreduce program to finish the multiplication step.
AB.r <- mapreduce(
 input = A.B,
 map = function(.,v){
 A = v[,1:2]
 B = v[,3:4]
 keyval(NULL, A*B)
}
)

It works but I have two questions.

1. After equijoin, I lost my key (118476480_1    118476480_7721 187108862_1    187108862_7721). The key is always NULL. Is there a way to keep the key I used to join as the key returned by equijoin since I may need it to do join work with other maps?

2. Are there any other efficient ways to code this task instead of joining two maps into one? I can use equijoin to join only two matrices. If there's operation involving with three or more independent matrices, then how should I handle them?

Thank you very much for any help.

Lan

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1332] Questions about equijoin
messages.body_plain:
equijoin takes a reduce argument, which takes three arguments, key, left side, right side. The default is rmr2:::reduce.default if you want to take a look, but it's complex because it's general. I think in your case a function such as

function (k, left, right) keyval(k, left *right)

should do the job.

As far as the three way join, of course you can do two equijoins. It's possible to generalize an equijoin to a multi-way join, but it's going to be complex. Maybe you can enter a feature request for the next rmr2 version, please use the issue tracker.

Even better, since you are not really dealing with big data, since it fits memory on a single machine, you should look into in-memory solutions that can give you better performance. I hope this helps.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: RMR2 VS Regular R Streaming
messages.body_plain:
Jonathan Seidman did a side by side implementation when he was at Orbitz and he has the results on his github account. Michael Smith reported on this very forum a 30X productivity improvement on a project that initially took a few months (but the order in which the two implementations were performed of course is a confounding factor). As far as speed, it depends what you write on top of streaming. If you write like me, it's even ;) But the amount of effort that goes into just one thing, accumulating the groups efficiently on the reduce side, you don't want to go through that if you don't have to, believe me.

Antonio

It looks like you don't have permissions to write to some directory in that path on HDFS. We are changing the default from the next version as reports like yours were starting to accumulate. Of course a new default is only an educated guess. The  best approach is to set the tmp directory with rmr.options(dfs.tempdir = "some writable path here"). It has to work for both backends, that is local file system and hdfs. That is far from ideal, so we are changing this from the next version, there's a setting from an hdfs tmpdir and for the local one it relies on R's own tmpdir.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: hdfs partitions and rhadoop
messages.body_plain:
The internet seems to support two views:

The standard input format doesn't support nested directories. Write your own or build a list of the actual files with a recursive list operation
Just use globs in the input

The two groups seem busy in a downvoting confrontation on Stackoverflow. It seems to me the second is easy enough to try so that the truth be settled on the globbing issue. Your input could be /data/folder/*  or /data/folder/*/* according to different oral traditions. Alternatively, you could use hdfs.ls <http://hdfs.ls> from the rhdfs package to build a vector of partitions and pass it to mapreduce as the input argument. I think it could be of general interest if you reported back on your solution. Thanks

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: hdfs partitions and rhadoop
messages.body_plain:
I am using an input filter as follows. That allows me to create a dyunamic partition in hive and subsequently filter based on that.

input.filter = function ( directory, filter, start, end )
{
    files  = hdfs.ls <http://hdfs.ls>( directory )$file
    filter = paste(directory, filter, sep='/')
    keys   = substr( files, nchar( filter ) + 1, 100 )
    files[ which (keys == start) : which( keys == end) ]
}

Works like a charm. The start and end tag can be passed through the command line.

messages.body_plain:
What you are doing looks reasonable to me so we need more information. Maybe you could add an rmr.str(gc()) in your reduce function. This will perform garbage collection but also print relevant information in stderr, which you can later access.  Also please provide the rmr and Hadoop version you are running. The golden standard is always to give me something I can run myself (complete program with input), and at least showing the code is the second best option. I am aware that in certain cases it's impossible, but then it becomes also impossible to debug a more than trivial problem.  Most likely R is allocating too much memory > 6gb. It could be an error in your code or an error in my code, and it's hard to separate the two without me tampering with the rmr2 build. Finally keep in mind that having a large number of small reduce groups is a slow programming pattern, just because the reduce function is an interpreted function. But one thing at a time, let's figure out the memory first, then the speed.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
I would suggest validating that the input to each reducer is indeed as small as you think it is. The logic is:
- There is a huge discrepancy between the the memory requirements, non-failing usage, and the size of allocated memory when the task fails.
- The process may be killed by the container before the R code starts running over that specific chunk of data.

A null / missing value for one of they the keys (happens a lot with real data...) will result in one key having lots and lots of data. Before you go into the rat-hole of profiling any further, I would recommend running a simplified version of your code that would count values per key, just to make sure you're not wasting your time.

Antonio,

It turned out that the reducers that failed with out-of-memory errors indeed were getting values that were larger. The job ran to completion when I put a threshold on the number of rows in the value in the reducer and returned NULL when the number of records exceeded the threshold. However, the largest value that a reducer got was a data frame of 3 * 10^5 rows and 10 columns (all the values were strings of about length 10).

Thanks for helping me debug this problem. I am still unsure as to why a reducer with such a small input finds 8GB insufficient. Also, I will upgrade to rmr2 soon. When I said "prefer" I wanted to know if rmr2 was tested only with only one of the versions of map reduce.

1. 하둡2.0을 가상서버로 Cluster 설정을 한 상태입니다.(Master : namenode, nodemanager, resourcemanager, secondarynamenode, datanode)(Slave : nodemanager, datanode) 이 위에다 rhdfs, rmr, rhbase를 설치하는게 맞나요? 그리고 rstudio는 필수적으로 활용되고 있나요?

2. R language is equivalent to R language on Hadoop?????? please let me know useful site/URL/pdf except GitHub and r-project.

3. I plan on testing. using the OpenAPI(input). please let me know cautions. Thank you

> Hi.. I'm student starting RHadoop. I have a questions.
>
> 1. I was set up l Hadoop2.0 on CentOS(Multi-node Cluster). on this status, install rhdfs /  rmr / rhbase right?

This question has no answer unless you provide versions of everything. Besides that, we can test only a few combinations so you have two options: install whatever combination we tested (Hadoop, OS and RHadoop packages) or try your own and run the tests yourselves to make sure the combination is compatible. Asking about a random combination of Hadoop, OS and rhadoop packages will get you the "we don't know" answer with high probability. Testing means running R CMD check. For rmr2, you need to install an additional package, quickcheck. That's it.

> and Rstudio is necessary generally?

No

>
> 2. R language is equivalent to R language on Hadoop?????? please let me know useful site/URL/pdf except GitHub and r-project.

Please define R language on Hadoop and equivalence of languages. Sorry, we put everything on github, documentation, code, you name it. messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#1393] Can input be a folder of Rdata files?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
unfortunately that's  not supposed to work. Hadoop needs a way to parse the data, at least to the point of telling where records start and the distinction between key and value. Inside that, it can be opaque as long as one doesn't need certain features. With Rdata we don't have that information, or at least  not in a format that Hadoop streaming can understand.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1392] Rhadoop on Cloudera's CHD4.6 and CentOS 4.6
messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#1392] Rhadoop on Cloudera's CHD4.6 and CentOS 4.6
messages.body_plain:
As you can tell from the compatibility page  <https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/rmr2/blob/3.1.0/docs/compatibility.md> we don't have that information. I am sure testing for some version of CDH will be added soon, but I can't guarantee the exact combination. Furthermore, we only test in distributed mode. You have two options: if you are building your cluster now and you want the least amount of trouble, pick one of the tested combinations; if you have an existing setup or are under certain constraints to support other software, just try it out. It is as simple as running R CMD check path-to-package-archive. If it passes all the tests, we call that compatible (some errors in the document building part can be ignored). Chances are that if you pick a reasonably modern combination of components, like the one you listed, it's going to pass the tests. If you do that and have the time to report back, that would be helpful for the project.

Antonio
